title: From task-specific networks to foundation models in diabetes care: a critical review of opportunities, evaluation gaps, and safety frontiers.
desc: [Frontiers in artificial intelligence] Artificial intelligence in diabetes care has historically relied on task-specific supervised learning, such as bespoke networks for retinopathy grading, kidney disease prediction, and glucose forecasting. The emergence of foundation models (FMs: large models pretrained on broad data, typically with self-supervision, and adapted to many downstream tasks) is displacing this paradigm across diabetes-relevant modalities: ophthalmic models such as RETFound, pretrained on 1.6 million retinal photographs, have been reported to outperform task-specific networks on retinopathy grading and systemic disease prediction, especially when labeled data are scarce; transformer-based time-series models are replacing long short-term memory (LSTM) pipelines for continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) forecasting; clinical large language models (LLMs) such as Med-PaLM and GPT-4 attain expert-level scores on medical question-answering benchmarks; and generative models supply synthetic CGM and electronic health record (EHR) data. This review provides a critical, modality-organized synthesis of this transition. We (i) formalize a three-era taxonomy: rule-based risk scores (era I), task-specific deep learning (era II, 2016-2020), and foundation models (era III, from 2021), and map the diabetes literature onto it; (ii) survey foundation-model architectures, pretraining objectives, and adaptation strategies across retinal imaging, CGM, longitudinal EHR, and multimodal data; (iii) expose an evaluation crisis: benchmark contamination of LLM medical evaluations, a near-universal absence in the literature we reviewed of external and prospective validation for retinal and CGM foundation models, miscalibration under dataset shift, and, to our knowledge and within the reviewed literature (January 2016-December 2025; negative findings are time-sensitive), the absence of any randomized evaluation of a foundation model in a diabetes workflow; and (iv) analyze safety risks: hallucinated insulin-dosing advice, automation bias, inherited algorithmic inequity, and privacy exposure during adaptation. We conclude that the decisive open problem is no longer representation learning but grounded, calibrated, causally informed deployment, requiring contamination-resistant evaluation, prospective trials, and hybrid architectures coupling foundation-model representations with treatment-effect estimation.

Artificial Intelligence in Skin Cancer Detection: Is Clinical Deployment Outpacing Experimental Validation?
desc: [Experimental dermatology] Deep neural networks classify dermoscopic and clinical images of skin lesions with accuracy that matches, and in curated comparisons exceeds, experienced dermatologists. Regulators have responded: an elastic scattering spectroscopy device with an embedded classifier is authorised for primary care in the United States, an image-based system has conditional approval in the National Health Service, and consumer applications are marketed directly to the public. In this Viewpoint we argue that clinical deployment is advancing faster than the experimental evidence that investigative dermatology would normally demand. Performance measured on internal test sets falls when algorithms are exposed to external images, non-dermoscopic photographs or other populations. Networks learn confounders, such as surgical ink markings, as readily as morphology, and the histopathological reference standard is itself subject to substantial observer variation. Public training datasets record skin phototype for about 2% of images and contain almost no darkest-phototype, acral or nail images. Regulated devices with prospective evidence achieve high sensitivity or negative predictive value at the cost of low specificity, shifting referral and biopsy rates with unmeasured effects on patient outcomes and overdiagnosis, and the single randomised trial to date improved diagnostic accuracy, chiefly among non-dermatologists, without measuring those outcomes. We identify where the largest gains lie, in primary care, allied health and under-served regions, and propose an experimental agenda: phototype-stratified external validation, shortcut-detection and counterfactual explanation studies, consensus histopathological labelling, pragmatic randomised trials with outcome endpoints reported to CONSORT-AI, and post-market surveillance under the European Medical Device Regulation and Artificial Intelligence Act.

Implementing Artificial Intelligence in Daily Clinical Practice, from Voice Dictation to Operating Room Organization: A Targeted Narrative Review with Hysteroscopy as a Clinical Exemplar.
desc: [Journal of clinical medicine] Artificial intelligence (AI) is entering routine care through documentation tools, decision support, and hospital operations. The central question is whether these systems improve clinical work and patient care once embedded in routine workflows, not only whether they perform well on test data. This targeted narrative review follows AI from voice dictation and ambient documentation to operating room (OR) organization, using hysteroscopy as a clinical exemplar of the transition from technical performance to clinical utility. Evidence identified through targeted searches completed on 6 September 2026 was appraised with a framework that distinguishes image-level from patient-level results, internal from independent validation, and discrimination from clinical utility. Randomized trials and multisite observational data show modest, product-dependent benefits of clinician-reviewed ambient documentation; inaccuracies persist. Evidence for patient-message drafting derives from ratings of responses to public-forum questions and supports only bounded, supervised feasibility testing. In hysteroscopy, selected models discriminate well in narrowly defined tasks, but most studies are retrospective, image-level, or internally validated, and patient-level errors in high-risk categories are seldom reported. Reported gains in OR scheduling come largely from simulation. Safe implementation requires a defined clinical need, baseline measurement, subgroup-aware local validation, accountable review, and predefined criteria for expansion or withdrawal.

Computer-Aided Drug Design for Immunosuppressive Tumor Microenvironment Reprogramming: A Critical Review.
source: PubMed · International journal of molecular sciences
desc: [International journal of molecular sciences] How can cellular interactions in solid tumors guide molecular interventions against immune suppression? This critical review examines how computer-aided drug design (CADD) connects immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) states to testable molecular hypotheses. We distinguish observational artificial intelligence (AI) predictions from molecular intervention hypotheses and examine the experimental evidence required to evaluate them. We reviewed patient-derived models, spatial and multi-omics profiling, molecular design, simulation, and pharmacology using literature identified through 15 October 2026. Adenosine-receptor antagonist discovery and generative protein-binder design illustrated how computational methods contributed to experimentally tested molecular candidates. Native-state structural studies, stromal delivery, and protein degradation broadened the approaches considered. We organized these findings into a proposed framework encompassing in vivo and patient-derived systems, multi-omics mapping, phenotyping of TME states, actionable AI integration, combination-therapy prioritization, and translational testing (IMPACT). A retrospective analysis of a phase III trial illustrated how the framework connects clinical outcomes to questions about mechanism, patient selection, and exposure. The synthesis clarifies the evidence required to connect molecular binding, target engagement, and exposure to patient benefit. IMPACT provides a structure for relating biological context to molecular design and specifying hypotheses for prospective evaluation.

title: Automated Detection of Abnormal Pediatric Electroencephalograms Using Machine Learning: Retrospective Study.
desc: [JMIR medical informatics] Electroencephalography (EEG) is widely used in medicine as a technique for the assessment of several brain-related pathologies. However, EEG interpretation requires specialized expertise and remains a labor-intensive task, particularly for prolonged recordings in intensive care, where timely expert review is often challenging. The aim of this study is to address this problem by using AI methods to automate EEG interpretation and compare the performance of different modeling approaches. A gradient boosting-based model, inspired by the work of Albaqami et al, was implemented and compared to deep learning (DL)-based models using convolutional neural networks to classify images generated from raw EEG signals. The models were trained and tested on pediatric EEGs acquired at the University Hospital in Essen. The DL model showed higher observed sensitivity (78.3%) and F1-score (80%) compared to the gradient boosting model (sensitivity: 65.2%; F1-score: 73.8%), indicating improved detection of abnormal EEGs. However, the gradient boosting approach achieved higher specificity (93% vs 89.6%), suggesting a stronger ability to recognize normal EEGs. Overall, both methods yielded promising results, with classification accuracies reaching up to 85.3%. Both approaches show potential for automated EEG interpretation. Future improvements, including larger and more diverse datasets, refined DL architectures, and integration of explainable AI techniques, could further enhance performance.

title: A comprehensive study of skin lesion segmentation and classification using deep learning techniques.
desc: [Frontiers in artificial intelligence] Deep learning has become an important computational approach in dermatology because it enables automated segmentation and classification of skin lesions. Manual dermoscopic analysis is time-consuming and depends on specialist expertise, with potential inter-observer variability. There is a need to develop reliable computer-aided diagnostic tools. This structured narrative review covers journal papers published mainly from 2018 to 2026 on skin lesion analysis with focus on image preprocessing, benchmark datasets, conventional machine learning approaches, convolutional neural networks, U-Net architectures, transfer learning approaches, Vision Transformers, attention-based models, ensemble solutions, and hybrid segmentation-classification systems. Building on present reviews covering individual tasks as well as broader segmentation-classification pipelines, the present work provides a critical development-to-deployment analysis connecting dataset characteristics, preprocessing, segmentation, classification, evaluation, explainability, robustness, fairness, computational requirements, and clinical applicability. The paper describes widely used evaluation metrics and explains why results obtained across different datasets, partitions, and experimental setups should not be directly compared. Major open problems include class imbalance, data bias, domain shift, limited representation of diverse skin tones, inadequate external validation, computational requirements, and limited explainability of efficient models. Emerging trends such as self-supervised learning, Transformers, foundation models, explainable AI, federated learning, and multi-modal clinical data are reviewed as well. The review offers practical advice to researchers and clinicians on how to approach the preprocessing, segmentation, classification, and evaluation of skin lesions and highlights priorities in developing clinically reliable skin lesion analysis systems.

title: AI Applications in Aortic and Peripheral Artery Disease: Risk Prediction, Imaging, Procedural Support, and Longitudinal Surveillance.
desc: [Methodist DeBakey cardiovascular journal] Aortic disease and lower-extremity peripheral artery disease (PAD) generate substantial morbidity, mortality, and longitudinal imaging burden. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly studied for vascular risk prediction, image analysis, procedural support, and surveillance, but the maturity of these applications is heterogeneous. This review evaluates recent AI applications in aortic disease and PAD, emphasizing the distinction between algorithmic performance, external validation, demonstrated workflow impact, and proven patient benefit. Automated image segmentation and opportunistic abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) detection have the most mature evidence base, including retrospective external validation and, for AI-assisted AAA case finding, nonrandomized evidence of improved downstream evaluation and follow-up. Conversely, while machine-learning models for vascular risk prediction and disease progression often report high retrospective accuracy, their clinical readiness remains strictly investigational. Across most aortic and PAD applications, there is a persistent lack of independent external validation, decision-curve analysis, and prospective testing against standard care. Image-fusion guidance has clinical evidence for reducing procedural resource use, but this evidence should not be conflated with autonomous AI or robotic navigation. Cardiovascular digital twins remain largely mechanistic, computational, or early-development frameworks. AI can augment vascular imaging and risk assessment, but high retrospective accuracy is not equivalent to clinical utility. Current guideline thresholds for repair, revascularization, and surveillance should not be altered on the basis of investigational radiomics or prediction models. Translation requires multicenter external validation, prospective workflow evaluation, calibration and net-benefit assessment, transparent reporting, and trials demonstrating improved patient outcomes.

title: Classification Performance of a Deep Learning Algorithm for Common Skin Lesions in the Emergency Department: A Multicenter Preliminary Validation Study.
desc: [Journal of clinical medicine] Background/Objectives: Initial classification of skin lesions in the emergency department (ED) is difficult when dermatology consultations are limited. This study externally validated a deep learning (DL) algorithm for classifying three common ED skin lesions and explored whether algorithmic pre-classification was associated with changes in the classification performance of medical staff. Methods: A ResNet-50-based algorithm was developed using 6000 clinical images from 4815 patients. For external validation, 100 images from an independent institution were classified by the algorithm and nine medical staff members (three emergency medicine specialists, three residents, and three physician assistant [PA] nurses). Fifteen days later, the staff reclassified the same randomly reordered images with the algorithmic pre-classification provided. Results: In external validation, the algorithm showed an overall accuracy of 0.96 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.90-0.99), lesion-specific balanced accuracies of 0.95-0.96, and a macro-average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.98 (95% CI, 0.95-1.00). Unassisted, the three PA nurses differed significantly from the algorithm for urticaria and herpes zoster (all p < 0.01, McNemar's exact test). After receiving algorithmic assistance, all medical staff showed a balanced accuracy of 0.97 or higher for all three lesions. In the mixed-effects model, assistance was associated with higher odds of correct classification (odds ratio 25.9, 95% CI 11.7-57.2), and inter-rater agreement (Fleiss' κ) increased from 0.70 to 0.97. Conclusions: The algorithm demonstrated high classification performance on independent external validation, and algorithmic assistance was associated with improved classification performance, with the largest absolute gains among medical staff with lower unassisted accuracy. As these findings are exploratory, they should be confirmed in randomized prospective studies.

title: Beyond chronological age: uncovering disease-dependent variability in AI-driven pediatric bone age assessment.
desc: [Insights into imaging] To assess performance and agreement of a commercial artificial intelligence (AI) tool relative to routine pediatric radiologists' bone age assessments in a large pediatric cohort, with focus on different groups of growth disorders. One thousand five hundred sixteen anterior-posterior hand radiographs of pediatric patients (50.6% boys, mean age 10.84 ± 3.66 years) were retrospectively analyzed using the AI tool BoneAge. AI results were compared with board-certified pediatric radiologists' reports using Bland-Altman plots, Spearman correlations, and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Subgroup analyses were performed for three major indications: genetic/neuroendocrine (n = 1179), orthopedic (n = 152), and oncologic disorders (n = 185). Mean absolute difference (MAD) in estimated bone age by radiologists and AI was 6.4 ± 7.0 months for the whole cohort, with complete concordance in 45.1% of cases. Best results were achieved in orthopedic questions with an MAD of 4.1 ± 5.6 months (genetic/neuroendocrine: 6.6 ± 7.2, oncologic: 6.7 ± 6.3 months). There was significant correlation between AI and radiologists for the whole study population (ρ = 0.980), and the three main groups: genetic/neuroendocrine (ρ = 0.974), orthopedic (ρ = 0.952), and oncologic indications (ρ = 0.988). ICCs for the entire cohort and the main indication groups were > 0.9, indicating excellent agreement between radiologist and AI. The investigated algorithm showed good agreement with bone age assessments performed by pediatric radiologists in a large pediatric cohort. Novel to previous studies, the indication for imaging was considered, demonstrating that agreement between algorithm output and radiologists' assessments varied across disease groups, with highest agreement observed in orthopedic indications. Software output differs according to disease groups, with best results for orthopedic indications. title: Multi-Reference Evaluation of Deep Learning Tumour Segmentation in Multi-Sequence Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma MRI.
desc: [Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland)] Background/Objectives: Deep learning segmentation of nasopharyngeal carcinoma is usually reported as one Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) against one reference mask, although multi-sequence MRI is often delineated separately on each sequence. We aimed to quantify how far the choice of reference changes reported performance, and to compare this with the disagreement between radiologists. Methods: We analysed a public dataset of 277 patient records with separately delineated T1-weighted, T2-weighted and contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI, 30 of whom were annotated by two radiologists. Tumour volumes were compared without registration. Spatial agreement was measured after rigid registration, with the loss from transferring masks between acquisition grids estimated separately. nnU-Net models were scored against every reference, including the second radiologist's, in 102 held-out patient records. Results: Without registration, the sequence effect on tumour volume was 10.9%, against a reader effect of 5.7% (ratio 1.9, 95% CI 1.40 to 2.49). After rigid registration, per-sequence references agreed at a median DSC of 0.783, against 0.898 between radiologists; in the double-annotated patient records, the paired gap narrowed only from 0.129 to 0.083 (95% CI 0.063 to 0.111) when grid transfer was matched. One fixed set of predictions scored 0.726, 0.685 and 0.673, depending only on the reference (median per-patient reference spread 0.075), and switching the reference sequence moved scores 2.7 to 3.6 times as much as switching the radiologist. Conclusions: Part of the cross-sequence difference is a difference in what each sequence makes visible rather than annotation error, so a single-reference DSC on multi-sequence data depends on a rarely stated choice. Performance should be reported against every available reference and read against measured inter-reader agreement.

title: Diagnostic factors influencing orthodontic extraction decision-making: a systematic review.
desc: [Frontiers in oral health] Orthodontic extraction decision-making requires integration of multiple diagnostic characteristics, yet the factors underlying extraction vs. non-extraction treatment selection have not been comprehensively synthesized across conventional clinical research and contemporary prediction models. This systematic review aimed to identify and critically evaluate the diagnostic factors influencing orthodontic extraction decisions and determine their consistency across the available evidence. PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception through July 2026 for studies evaluating diagnostic factors associated with orthodontic extraction decisions or statistical or artificial intelligence-based prediction models. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment. Substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis, and findings were synthesized narratively. Nineteen studies met the inclusion criteria. Dental crowding and tooth size -arch length discrepancy were the most consistently evaluated diagnostic factors but were typically considered alongside facial profile, incisor position, skeletal relationships, and occlusal characteristics. No consistent numerical threshold for recommending extraction was identified. Artificial intelligence-based prediction models demonstrated promising performance, with interpretable predictors substantially overlapping with diagnostic variables identified in conventional clinical studies. Methodological quality ranged from moderate to critical risk of bias, with most prediction-model studies judged to be at high risk of bias. These findings indicate that orthodontic extraction decision-making is fundamentally multifactorial rather than governed by a single diagnostic measurement or threshold. Current artificial intelligence models should be considered decision-support tools pending higher-quality prospective research and external validation; whether image-derived or latent features provide genuinely novel determinants of extraction need remains uncertain. https://osf.io/x86zy.

title: Dendritic structure enables powerful plasticity.
desc: [Current research in neurobiology] Over the past decades, it has become increasingly clear that the complex morphology of cortical neurons is more than just a quirk of evolution, and that dendritic compartments serve as computational elements in their own right, rather than just providing connections between nerve cell bodies. While most computational studies discuss the enhanced representational capabilities of multi-compartment models as compared to point neurons, we focus here on the implications of neuronal morphology for synaptic plasticity. We argue that the ability of single neurons to simultaneously encode multiple pieces of information gives synapses local access to more than just the classical Hebbian pre- and postsynaptic terms, and with much greater specificity and reaction speed than permitted by other globally modulated factors. Based on a comparative review of recent dendritic learning models, we show how such neuronal compartmentalization can provide synapses with the means for calculating various forms of error signals, which in turn give rise to powerful real-time and fully local instantiations of deep learning through gradient descent. Implemented within cortical microcircuits capable of propagating and manipulating these errors, compartmentalized neurons thus ultimately enable the learning of far more complex tasks than are achievable by globally modulated Hebbian plasticity alone.

title: AI and the Responsibility-Bearing Status of Authorship.
desc: [Philosophy & technology] Generative AI has sharpened an old question: who, or what, can be an author? The central aim of this paper is to reconstruct the conception of authorship already implicit in copyright law. I argue that copyright encodes authorship as a responsibility-bearing status, constituted by a cluster of conditions: intentional agency, guided control, and relational expression (ACE). The paper's contribution is to make that conception explicit, to show that the human-authorship rule is best understood as a proxy for those capacities, not a species predicate, and to explain why this generates a tension with recognizing current generative AI systems as authors unless one is prepared to attribute to them the thicker agential capacities ACE requires. On that basis, the paper also clarifies why AI-assisted works may still be human-authored, while some AI-generated outputs give rise to genuine authorship gaps.

title: Digital twin oncology and multi-omics-driven artificial intelligence models for personalized drug response prediction: A systematic survey of emerging computational paradigms and clinical implementation challenges.
desc: [Computational biology and chemistry] The increasing complexity of tumor heterogeneity and variable therapeutic response has intensified the need for accurate personalized drug response prediction in oncology. Traditional trial-and-error chemotherapy strategies often result in suboptimal outcomes, toxicity, and delayed therapeutic adjustments. Rapid advances in multi-omics technologies, artificial intelligence (AI) and digital twin modeling have significantly reshaped computational oncology research. This survey systematically reviews peer-reviewed research and review articles published from 2021 onward that investigate emerging computational paradigms integrating digital twins and multi-omics AI for drug response prediction. The foundational concepts in digital twin oncology, multi-omics profiling and AI-driven precision medicine are outlined initially. The existing approaches are categorized into four major paradigms such as omics-driven machine learning models, deep learning based multimodal architectures, mechanistic digital twin simulation frameworks and hybrid digital twin AI systems enabling adaptive therapy optimization. The multi-omics data integration strategies, including early, intermediate, late, network-based and graph/pathway-based fusion techniques. The survey synthesizes recent developments in drug sensitivity prediction, immunotherapy response modeling, tumor evolution forecasting and virtual clinical trials, while critically analyzing challenges related to data heterogeneity, interpretability, generalization, privacy, regulatory compliance and ethical considerations. Finally, future directions are highlighted such as real-time adaptive digital twins, federated learning, explainable AI and regulatory ready clinical deployment frameworks. Overall, this review provides a structured taxonomy, comparative analysis and research roadmap for advancing integrated digital twin and multi omics AI systems toward clinically actionable precision oncology.

title: Causally Constrained and Uncertainty-Aware Cardiopulmonary Risk Prediction
desc: Routine chest computed tomography (CT) captures pulmonary, cardiac, and vascular phenotypes that jointly stratify lung cancer and cardiovascular disease, the two leading causes of death in lung-screening populations. Yet clinical risk calculators evaluate each disease in isolation and omit CT findings, whereas unconstrained machine learning overfits small hospital cohorts, learns treatment- and illness-confounded risk directions, and conceals uncertainty when patient records are incomplete. Here we present the Causal Envelope Agent (CE-Agent), a two-stage framework that compiles peer-reviewed epidemiological evidence into explicit constraints on risk-factor weights before any outcome is seen, while estimating local baseline risk and newly added CT phenotypes from cohort data. At deployment, closed-form uncertainty propagation accounts for missing clinical or CT inputs within milliseconds per patient, running over two orders of magnitude faster than Monte Carlo sampling and returning calibrated risk intervals that direct chart review and selective imaging to borderline patients. Across 53,452 lung-screening participants from 33 US hospitals and 6,814 multi-ethnic adults, CE-Agent outperforms cardiovascular calculators in lung screening, exceeds the Pooled Cohort Equations on hard atherosclerotic events while correcting their 1.7-fold risk overestimation, and generalizes from a single hospital or CT scanner to external sites while lowering required sample sizes up to fivefold. Applied unchanged to lung cancer, CE-Agent matches established screening models with accurate calibration even when restricted to risk-factor directions alone, and pairing both predictions improves joint cardiopulmonary triage from a single screening visit.

title: LabARIA: A Multi-Agent System for Integrative Analytics in Clinical Laboratories
desc: Background Laboratory medicine underpins clinical decision-making across nearly every care setting. Clinical laboratory errors and delays can compromise diagnostic reliability and patient care. However, laboratory quality and operational data are commonly reviewed through separate manual workflows, limiting timely recognition of emerging problems across complementary data sources. Methods We developed and evaluated LabARIA (Laboratory Agentic Reasoning and Integrative Analytics), a multi-agent AI system for coordinated surveillance of specimen workflows, analytical quality control, and laboratory operations. We conducted a single-center retrospective system development and evaluation at NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital/Weill Cornell Medical Center using laboratory data collected from May 1 through June 18, 2026, including 177,480 specimen-panel records, 75,103 internal quality-control (IQC) measurements, 633 proficiency-testing challenges, and 422 recalibration or maintenance actions. Forecasting agents were evaluated using patient-result streams with controlled perturbations, and synthetic staffing and inventory data. We assessed specimen rejection, cancellation, and turnaround-time patterns; warning recall and lead time before documented laboratory actions; assay-specific patient-based real-time quality control (PBRTQC) performance; and exploratory operational forecasting discrimination. Findings LabARIA characterized specimen and workflow patterns across clinical units and time periods, including hemolysis-related potassium rejections in the intensive care unit during early morning hours (49 of 367 tests [13.3%]). For analytical quality monitoring, the IQC agent generated warnings before 407 of 422 recorded QC actions (recall, 0.964 [95% CI, 0.942-0.978]), with a median lead time of 5.40 days (95% CI, 3.75-6.07). PBRTQC agent selected different monitoring strategies across 35 analytes. In a separate analysis, adding PBRTQC increased action recall from 0.964 to 0.993 (95% CI, 0.979-0.998). A dashboard presented tiered alerts for human review, and an accompanying chatbot supported interactive exploration of the summaries. For the operational forecasting module, areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve for 7-day inventory and staffing risk forecasting were 0.800 (95% CI, 0.696-0.881) and 0.877 (95% CI, 0.778-0.950), respectively. title: Inferring single-cell gene expression profiles from multicellular spatial transcriptomics data with st2sc
desc: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) enables the quantitative measurement of gene expression within tissue sections but is currently limited in spatial resolution, as each spot aggregates signals from multiple cells. Recovering single-cell gene expression profiles from these multicellular measurements requires two steps: explicit identification of individual cells and accurate estimation of per-gene expression. While existing methods have demonstrated the feasibility of recovering single-cell expression profiles, accurately estimating gene-level expression for individual cells remains an important challenge. To address this challenge, we propose st2sc (Spatial Transcriptomics to Single-Cell), an end-to-end framework for inferring single-cell gene profiles from multicellular ST data. st2sc introduces a novel Attention Gradient Flow Tracking (AGFT) algorithm that extracts attention maps from a Vision-Gene Transformer to identify candidate cell instances without predefined background constraints. The detected instances are then used by a set of regressors trained under a multiple-instance, multiple-target regression setting to predict precise single-cell gene expression counts. Comprehensive evaluations on synthetic and Visium-like datasets demonstrate that st2sc significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accurately segmenting cellular instances and predicting gene counts. The method can further resolve contested 2um bin in Visium HD. Application to human IPF lung showed the model can recover the subtype marker level analysis. This advancement further improves single-cell resolution analysis in spatial transcriptomics, facilitating more accurate downstream biological analyses.

Current Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Surgical Planning for Craniosynostosis: A Scoping Review.
desc: [ANZ journal of surgery] Craniosynostosis, the premature fusion of cranial sutures, can cause abnormal skull shapes, neurological issues and aesthetic concerns. Surgical correction is standard, but planning is complex and operator-dependent. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers the potential to enhance diagnosis, optimise planning and predict postoperative outcomes. A scoping review following PRISMA-ScR guidelines identified 11 studies involving paediatric patients with craniosynostosis. AI methods included unsupervised machine learning, convolutional neural networks, finite element models and variational autoencoders. Applications encompassed cranial severity scoring, phenotype classification, preoperative surgical simulation, intraoperative guidance and outcome prediction. AI-derived metrics correlated strongly with expert assessments, facilitated patient-specific planning and predicted postoperative aesthetics. AI is a transformative adjunct in craniosynostosis surgery. Clinically, it improves diagnostic accuracy, supports personalised surgical planning and guides intraoperative decision-making. Some studies show AI can contribute to better functional and aesthetic outcomes, showing great promise in the paediatric surgical field. Although AI does not replace clinical expertise, it enhances precision and reproducibility. Future research should prioritise prospective validation, integration into surgical workflows and development of interpretable, surgeon-friendly AI tools to maximise clinical benefit.

title: A thorough review on Deep Learning approaches to 2D-to-3D Registration in Medical Imaging
desc: 2D-to-3D image registration is a key component for several medical imaging purposes such as intraoperative guidance, enabling the alignment between preoperative 3D volumes and real-time 2D images. While conventional optimisation-based methods often struggle with non-convex objectives, sensitivity to initialisation, and high computational demands, deep learning (DL) has emerged as a promising alternative, offering improved alignment robustness and the potential for real-time performance. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of DL frameworks developed to address the challenges inherent in 2D-to-3D registration. We first outline how core concepts of DL are adapted to the registration problem. We then examine recent methodological advancements from multiple perspectives, including pipeline design, architectural innovations, and domain adaptation strategies. Particular attention is given to quantitative metrics, highlighting how performance is defined and measured across studies. Across the 41 included studies, we find that direct regression is the most common pipeline (23 studies, against 18 iterative ones), that hybrid CNN-attention architectures are gaining ground, and that research remains heavily concentrated on X-ray-to-CT registration. We conclude by identifying the absence of per-case uncertainty estimation and the strong neglect of temporal or sequential modelling as the two methodological gaps most consequential for clinical readiness, and discuss state-space models as a way to add temporal memory within intraoperative latency budgets. Further opportunities lie in more principled domain adaptation and in the integration of foundation models for representation learning.

title: Effect of Data Preprocessing Decisions on Sepsis-3 Labels in MIMIC-III and eICU-CRD: A Sensitivity Analysis
desc: Objective: Published Sepsis-3 detection rates range from 3.4 % to 65.2 % in MIMIC-III and from 9.8 % to 47.9 % in eICU-CRD. We tested whether data preprocessing decisions alone produce differences of this magnitude when data, cohort and sepsis definition are held fixed. Materials and Methods: Using the MIMIC-III and eICU-CRD databases we developed and applied a configurable pipeline (medalabel) that stepwise maps the databases into the OMOP Common Data Model, standardizes and cleans the data, and preprocesses them to compute Sepsis-3 labels. Each setting of the preprocessing represents one decision of published Sepsis-3 implementations, and settings can be freely combined. On fixed cohorts of first ICU stays (13,388 in MIMIC-III, 94,782 in eICU-CRD), we changed one setting of a reference configuration at a time (51 variants in five preprocessing domains) and compared detection rates and septic stays (Jaccard index) with the reference. We approximately reconstructed six published pipelines and combined the settings with the largest effects in pairs to test whether their effects add up. The time a value is measured can differ from the time it is documented and thus available for automated analysis. Beyond the usual retrospective view based on measurement time, the pipeline optionally combines both time points to simulate a real-time system. Results: The reference configuration labelled 31.5 % of ICU stays in MIMIC-III and 8.2 % in eICU-CRD as septic. Changing a single setting resulted in sepsis detection rates of 15.3-58.6 % in MIMIC-III and 4.6-17.2 % in eICU-CRD. The largest shifts from the reference, all in the same direction in both databases, came from the SOFA baseline, up to +27.1 percentage points (pp) in MIMIC-III and +9.0 pp in eICU-CRD, from disabling imputation (-16.3 and -2.5 pp), the temporal window (+12.6 and +5.3 pp) and aggregation (-10.1 and -0.8 pp); clinician-validated parameter sets had little effect (-4.8 and -1.1 pp). Even variants that changed the rate by less than 2 pp labelled partly different patients, with Jaccard indices as low as 0.67 in MIMIC-III and 0.56 in eICU-CRD (1 = identical septic stays). Reconstructions deviated from the published rates by 2-10 pp. Two settings applied together deviated from the sum of their single effects by 0.9-11.8 pp in MIMIC-III and by up to 4.9 pp in eICU-CRD. Simulating a real-time system lowered the MIMIC-III rate by 5.0 pp and delayed the label in 45 % of the stays that remained septic. Discus
