Advanced drug delivery strategies for overcoming tumor-mediated molecular hijacking: Emerging nanotherapeutics, advanced biotherapeutics, and artificial intelligence.
source: PubMed · Drug delivery and translational research
desc: [Drug delivery and translational research] Recent advances in precision oncology fueled the development of nanotherapeutics,​ molecularly targeted drugs, engineered immunotherapies, RNA therapeutics, and smart biomaterials for more selective cancer treatment. However, long-term therapeutic responses remain restricted by interconnected adaptive mechanisms, including ABC transporter-mediated drug efflux, dysregulated signaling pathways, apoptosis evasion, immune escape, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and tumor microenvironment​ remodeling. In this review article, these processes are collectively framed as tumor-mediated molecular hijacking, describing malignant cell exploitation and microenvironmental pathways that promote multidrug resistance and therapeutic failure. The review critically examines nanotherapeutic and advanced biotherapeutic strategies to counteract these mechanisms, including functionalized nanocarriers, antibody-drug conjugates, CAR-T cells, tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy, immune checkpoint blockade, mesenchymal stem-cell (MSC)-based therapeutics, CRISPR-mediated genome editing, bispecific T-cell engagers, and RNA-based approaches. Particular focus includes drug-delivery elements such as tumour penetration, intracellular trafficking, controlled release, pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and critical formulation attributes, as well as translational challenges such as manufacturability, scalability, reproducibility, stability, safety, and regulatory feasibility. Emerging biofabrication approaches enable the fabrication of adaptive and personalized delivery systems, while artificial intelligence and machine learning are utilized as tools for structure-guided design, nanocarrier optimization, treatment-response prediction, and patient-specific digital-twin modelling. This paper combines tumor-mediated molecular hijacking with drug delivery technology at the forefront and translational aspects to create a comprehensive platform for clinically relevant precision cancer therapeutics.Clinical trial number: Not applicable.

title: A Tumour-Aware Multimodal Framework for Explainable Prediction of IDH Mutation in Gliomas from Multi-Sequence MRI
desc: Accurate prediction of isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation status is essential for glioma diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning. Although recent deep learning approaches have demonstrated promising performance, many rely on whole-brain feature extraction and provide limited interpretability. This study proposes a tumour-aware multimodal framework for explainable, non-invasive prediction of IDH mutation status from multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The proposed framework integrates four MRI sequences (T1, T1CE, T2, and FLAIR), tumour subregion segmentation, quantitative radiomic descriptors, and clinical information within a unified deep learning architecture. An ablation study was conducted to evaluate the contribution of tumour-aware learning, radiomic features, and clinical variables. Model performance was assessed using multiple complementary evaluation metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, balanced accuracy, receiver operating characteristic analysis, confusion matrix evaluation, and Grad-CAM visualisation. Experimental results demonstrated that the proposed multimodal framework consistently outperformed the baseline MRI-only model, with the Clinical Fusion model achieving the strongest overall predictive performance. The integration of tumour-aware learning, radiomic descriptors, and clinical information progressively improved classification performance, while Grad-CAM visualisations indicated that the model predominantly focused on biologically relevant tumour regions. These findings suggest that tumour-aware multimodal feature integration enables accurate, interpretable, and non-invasive molecular profiling of gliomas and provides a promising foundation for future clinical decision support in precision neuro-oncology.

title: AI时代，文科可以这样“开疆拓土”
Smart Technologies in the Management of Metabolic Syndrome and Oral Health: A Narrative Review.
desc: [Healthcare (Basel, Switzerland)] Background/Objectives: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) and periodontitis are two of the most common chronic conditions sharing an underlying mechanism represented by systemic inflammation. Smart technologies, including machine learning (ML), wearable and Internet of Things (IoT) devices, telemedicine and intraoral sensors, are increasingly used in both fields. This narrative review examined how these technologies are used to predict, monitor and manage MetS and oral diseases and what evidence supports combining oral and metabolic data. Methods: Following the SANRA framework, PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science were searched for English-language articles published between January 2021 and May 2026. Of the 6922 records identified (3520 after de-duplication), 1852 were screened by title and abstract, and studies were selected by relevance to three research questions. Applications were classified by their current level of evidence. Results: ML models for MetS prediction often reported high discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] up to 0.99), but most were validated only internally, and several used the diagnostic components of MetS as predictors. Wearable, telemedicine and mobile interventions, usually combined with lifestyle programs, were associated with improvements in body weight, blood pressure and glycemic markers; artificial intelligence tools for dental imaging showed accuracy comparable to clinicians in mostly retrospective studies, with limited evidence on patient outcomes. Few studies combined oral and metabolic data: cross-sectional ML studies identified periodontal severity as a predictor of MetS and metabolic conditions as predictors of periodontitis, and salivary glucose correlated with blood glucose mainly in people living with diabetes, which does not establish diagnostic accuracy. No prospective study has tested an integrated dental-medical pathway. Conclusions: Integrating oral and metabolic data through smart technologies is biologically plausible and appears technically feasible, but its added diagnostic value, clinical effectiveness and cost effectiveness have not been established. Externally validated models, prospective cohorts and trials of integrated care pathways are required before routine use.

title: Cracks in Embeddings: Robustness and Stability of JEPA-Based Chest X-Ray Representations
desc: Self-supervised Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) models are increasingly used for medical imaging, however there is a limited understanding about robustness of these models toward real-world image changes. We test four JEPA-based chest X-ray encoders, trained on 78,468 NIH ChestX-ray14 images, under six tests: two black-box adversarial attacks (SPSA, Boundary Attack), three image corruptions (Gaussian noise, brightness shift, contrast shift), and a label-scarcity test, measuring embedding change and classification AUROC. These perturbations cause severe, model-dependent damage: encoder-level Cosine Similarity drops as low as 0.33, and AUROC falls by as much as 0.12 in the worst case (I-JEPA under the Boundary Test). We test two ways of training the small predictor on top of each frozen encoder to address this. Adversarial fine-tuning, trained on clean and perturbed images together, raises embedding consistency above 0.97 in nearly every case and improves AUROC, relative to the same perturbed baseline, for most models, with the largest gain of $+0.10$ on I-JEPA. A Vector-Quantized codebook method, trained only on clean images and evaluated on perturbed test images for the first time, instead degrades under distortion for all four models, most noticeably for I-JEPA ($-0.15$ AUROC on average), showing that its discrete bottleneck alone does not provide the robustness that comes from training on perturbed data directly.

title: AI-enabled drug repurposing in Alzheimer's disease: from computational nomination to pharmacological proof.
desc: [Frontiers in pharmacology] Artificial intelligence (AI) has expanded the scale and speed of drug repurposing in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Transcriptomic signature matching, network-based systems pharmacology, real-world data pharmacoepidemiology and multi-omics machine learning have generated hundreds of candidate drugs, while repurposed agents account for 35% (56 of 158) of drugs and 42% (15 of 36) of Phase 3 agents in the 2026 AD pipeline. Clinical translation, however, remains unproven. Randomised trials of GLP-1 receptor agonists illustrate the gap between prioritisation and therapeutic proof: semaglutide did not slow clinical progression in evoke and evoke+, while liraglutide did not improve the primary FDG-PET endpoint in ELAD. We examine four complementary evidence domains, defining what each can and cannot establish, and position large language models as a cross-cutting tool for evidence synthesis and knowledge-graph reasoning rather than an independent source of biological evidence. Rather than cataloguing methods and candidates, we appraise leading drugs at the individual-molecule level and propose explicit criteria for progression from computational nomination to clinical testing. The framework defines seven requirements for clinical progression: disease-stage matching, adequate site-of-action exposure, including CNS exposure for central mechanisms, mechanistic validation in human-relevant models, biomarker-stratified trial design, convergence across independent evidence domains, causal inference with explicit boundary conditions, and mechanism-aligned endpoints with predefined stopping rules. AI has improved candidate prioritisation in AD, but clinical value will depend on converting ranked hypotheses into pharmacologically plausible and prospectively testable programmes.

title: PADSNet: Physics-Aware Dual-Stream Network with Biomechanical Priors for Laryngeal Lesion Classification
desc: Precise classification of laryngeal lesions is clinically crucial yet highly challenging, as inter-class visual differences are often subtle. While abnormalities in vocal fold vibratory dynamics provide complementary discriminative information, existing deep learning models predominantly rely on visual appearance and lack explicit mechanisms for modeling clinically meaningful vibratory dynamics. To address this, we propose PADSNet, a Physics-Aware Dual-Stream Network for laryngeal lesion classification that integrates visual representations with explicit biomechanical reasoning. Specifically, a Wavelet-Attention Enhancement Module (WAEM) is designed to bridge the spectral-semantic gap, enabling complementary learning of spatial texture and dynamic frequency representations. Meanwhile, a Knowledge Computing Module (KCM) extracts interpretable biomechanical indices from temporal glottal distance waveforms, including indicators of mobility, symmetry, glottal closure, and vibration stability. These descriptors are subsequently incorporated into a Physics-Aware Gating Module (PAGM) as biomechanical priors to adaptively recalibrate visual feature toward pathology-relevant vibratory patterns. Extensive experiments on a clinical dataset demonstrate that PADSNet achieves an accuracy of 0.8452, an F1-score of 0.8090, a sensitivity of 0.7953, and a specificity of 0.8866. These results indicate that explicitly integrating biomechanical priors with deep visual representations provides a more accurate, robust, and clinically interpretable framework for automated laryngeal lesion classification.

title: CT-based machine learning and multimodal prediction in acute pancreatitis: a narrative review.
desc: [Abdominal radiology (New York)] Acute pancreatitis (AP) has a highly variable clinical course. This narrative review focuses on computed tomography (CT) radiomics, deep learning and clinical-imaging models for severity and adverse-outcome prediction, with clinical-only models as context. A targeted PubMed search checked on 16 October 2026, with a publication cutoff of 14 October 2026, retrieved 80 unique records; ten CT-informed exemplars and eight clinical-context studies were selected for detailed comparison. This is a representative, non-exhaustive synthesis. For severe AP (SAP) prediction, reported same-center internal or temporal areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) ranged from 0.852 to 0.894, and reported external-test AUCs from 0.887 to 0.916; one validation cohort of unconfirmed independence had an AUC of 0.920. These descriptive ranges do not establish model superiority or characterize all retrieved studies. CT protocols and input timing, endpoint definitions, sampling and validation designs varied. Predominantly retrospective evidence, uncertain prediction landmarks, incomplete calibration and threshold reporting, and limited prospective impact assessment constrain translation. Feature explanations describe model associations rather than causal intervention targets. Imaging artificial intelligence (AI) remains an adjunct to clinical assessment; independent validation, calibration, decision-curve appraisal and prospective workflow/outcome evaluation are needed before clinical-pathway integration.

title: Astrocyte Biocomputing: Astrocytic Contributions to Neural Network Computation
desc: Conductors are critical for the performance of an orchestra even though they do not emit sound. Basic research and clinical studies in the last decade are revealing that astrocytes may be the "conductors" of the "orchestra" that is the brain network: astrocytes make up approximately $50\%$ of all brain cells but do not emit electrical signals. Nevertheless, they may play critical roles in important cognitive brain functions, specifically learning, memory, and information processing. Here we consider the implications of these discoveries for brain-inspired machine learning (ML), where analogy is typically drawn between neurons and their electrical interactions. We highlight specific algorithms for two key astrocyte characteristics. The first characteristic is the ability to link to and modulate thousands of synapses simultaneously. A model based on this characteristic yields faster training and makes the network more robust to noise, providing a supervised learning algorithm that can be applied to any existing neural network. The second characteristic we focus on is that the non-electrical communication among astrocytes includes slow, rhythmic dynamics. The rhythmic sharing algorithm we developed based on this premise yields rapid anomaly detection adaptation and prevents catastrophic forgetting. Overall, we find that astrocyte-derived algorithms outperform neurocentric algorithms significantly and remediate critical weaknesses of current state-of-the-art ML models.

title: Artificial intelligence-enhanced electrocardiography for detection and prediction of dilated cardiomyopathy.
desc: [European heart journal] A major challenge in dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) care is the identification and management of individuals at risk before disease manifestation. An artificial intelligence (AI) model applied to electrocardiography (ECG) was developed to detect and predict the echocardiographic DCM phenotype (left ventricular dilatation with systolic dysfunction) and was evaluated for its ability to stratify the risk of incident DCM in familial cohorts. A deep learning model was trained to detect the echocardiographic DCM phenotype and to predict its future onset, using more than 330 000 ECG-echocardiogram pairs from the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston. Model performance was validated in cohorts from the UK Biobank, Zhongshan Hospital, and Antwerp University Hospital, and compared with models based on traditional ECG features and echocardiographic traits. To assess performance in familial DCM, genetically predisposed individuals identified through cascade screening at the cardiogenetics clinics of Antwerp University Hospital (n = 166, 18% DCM positive) and Maastricht University Medical Center (n = 177, 18% DCM positive) were evaluated. The AI-ECG model achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of .87-.97 for diagnosing the prevalent DCM phenotype, outperforming traditional ECG parameters. AI-ECG was comparable to echocardiography for predicting future DCM (C-index .80-.87 and .80-.90, respectively). In familial cohorts, 5-year negative predictive values were 95.5% (Antwerp) and 91.5% (Maastricht), with corresponding positive predictive values of 42.4% and 39.4%, while high-risk scores were associated with a 5.1-6.4-fold increased risk of incident DCM. The explainable AI-ECG model detects the echocardiographic DCM phenotype and predicts future disease, and supports the exclusion of short- to mid-term disease in genetically at-risk individuals. This low-cost tool could help reduce surveillance burden and facilitate earlier intervention.

title: X-Strata: Separating Aneurysms and Overlapping Vessels into Layers from 2D X-ray Angiography
desc: An X-ray angiogram sums every structure along a ray into one pixel. When vessels cross an aneurysm, they obscure part of it and mix their contrast into its filling curve. We present X-Strata, a network that separates a cine angiogram into three layers: the complete aneurysm sac, the vessels in front of it, and the vessels behind it. Contrast timing indicates how much each layer contributes to a pixel, and parallax between two views indicates their order, which a single view cannot determine. X-Strata first estimates the layers and their contrast curves, then uses the second view to assign vessels to the front or back layer, and lifts all layers into 3D. It learns from layer labels projected from same-session 3D rotational angiography, but needs only 2D cine runs and their acquisition geometry at inference. On 220 held-out patients from three centers (122 external), two-view X-Strata ranks first among 14 baselines, including VGGT and C$^2$RV, in recovering the sac where vessels overlap it (Dice 0.693 internal, 0.641 external) and in ordering the layers (balanced accuracy 0.703, 0.659). Its order accuracy exceeds that of all 11 end-to-end baselines by at least 4.1 points internally and 3.3 externally (Holm-adjusted $p < 0.001$) and grows with view separation. Recovered 3D sac surfaces have a median Chamfer distance of 0.34 mm on the internal cohort. X-Strata may therefore provide layered aneurysm and vessel information, including 3D sac shape, for patients who undergo only 2D angiography.

title: Artificial intelligence for Traditional Chinese Medicine classic formula development: a technology readiness assessment using metabolic syndrome as a case study.
desc: [Frontiers in pharmacology] Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) formulas, developed through millennia of clinical practice, represent a rich legacy of approximately 100,000 documented prescriptions (99,584 named formula entries in the second edition of the Dictionary of Traditional Chinese Medicine Formulas), yet on average fewer than ten new TCM products were approved annually by China's NMPA from 2013 to 2024 (77 approvals in total). The experience-based screening paradigm is misaligned with the precision medicine framework demanded by metabolic syndrome (MetS), a multi-target disorder affecting an estimated 1.54 billion adults (95% CrI 1.35-1.76) in 2023. Although artificial intelligence (AI)-encompassing knowledge graphs (KGs), large language models (LLMs), and high-throughput experimentation-has been proposed as a solution, its actual readiness for TCM development remains unclear. This review critically examines KG, LLM, and high-throughput validation technologies enabling precision phytomedicine for MetS, providing a realistic roadmap for AI-driven TCM research and development. The three technology streams exhibit asymmetric readiness. At the stream level, knowledge-graph approaches span Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 3-6, large language model approaches span TRL 1-5, and high-throughput validation platforms span TRL 3-5. LLM development is limited by three TCM-specific hallucination types that lack evaluation benchmarks. KG entity recognition is the most mature component, yet reasoning is hindered by the absence of negative data, missing dose-time dimensions, and unencoded monarch-minister-assistant-envoy hierarchies. High-throughput platforms are technically feasible but remain mismatched to MetS functional endpoints-tumor-derived organoid paradigms show limited direct transferability and would require substantial adaptation. Precision phytomedicine must follow a "foundations before algorithms" sequence: institutionalize negative data, build TCM-Hallu benchmarks, establish functional-endpoint evaluation, and develop AI-assisted regulatory review. Algorithmic advances will remain in an incomplete information space until knowledge infrastructure gaps are closed.

title: QCAP-VQA: Question-Conditioned Capped Prior-Mass Supervision for Medical Visual Question Answering
desc: Medical visual question answering models can answer correctly without attending to the anatomy that the question names. Automatic region priors allow spatial supervision without expert masks, but they are noisy, and it is unclear how strongly they should shape attention and how their effect should be verified. We present QCAP-VQA, which supervises a subset of cross-attention heads with a question-conditioned prior built from ranked segmentation proposals. Its capped prior-mass objective penalizes insufficient attention inside the prior only below a threshold. We evaluate attention against SLAKE structure boxes that play no role in training, separating attention on the named anatomy from how attention shifts between questions about the same image. QCAP-VQA matches the accuracy of a baseline without spatial supervision (84.26% vs. 84.23%), and every evaluated prior-supervised model places more attention on the annotated structures. Over a 64-fold range of regularization strength, the capped objective keeps prior mass between 0.67 and 0.77, whereas a pooled region-mass objective drives it to 0.97 and loses accuracy. The cost lies in question conditioning: as the constraint widens or strengthens, attention shifts agree less with the expert-defined contrast. Across 13 configurations, prior-referenced and expert-referenced evaluation rank the models in largely opposite order (Spearman correlation of -0.87), and the capped models it favors track the prior's own errors. Because clinical use of medical visual question answering requires answers grounded in the queried anatomy, supervision from automatic priors should be judged against independent anatomical references.

title: Multimodal Risk Stratification and Surveillance for Gastric Cancer in Chronic Atrophic Gastritis and Gastric Intestinal Metaplasia: Integrating Histology, Endoscopy, Biomarkers, and Artificial Intelligence.
desc: [Clinical and experimental gastroenterology] Gastric cancer remains a major global health burden, and chronic atrophic gastritis (CAG) and gastric intestinal metaplasia (GIM) are important premalignant conditions. The risk of progression, however, varies considerably between individuals, making reliable risk stratification central to decisions on surveillance. Histological staging remains the most established approach. In a recent meta-analysis of prospective cohorts, Operative Link on Gastritis Assessment (OLGA) stages III-IV and OLGIM (Operative Link on Gastric Intestinal Metaplasia Assessment) stages III-IV were associated with substantially higher risks of gastric cancer than stages 0-II, with risk ratios of 32.31 and 12.38, respectively. Endoscopic assessment adds information on the distribution of mucosal abnormalities and can improve biopsy targeting; an EGGIM score >4 has shown 95.7% sensitivity and 91.4% specificity for identifying OLGIM stages III-IV. Helicobacter pylori eradication reduces subsequent gastric cancer risk, but surveillance remains necessary in patients with advanced atrophy, extensive GIM, or previous gastric neoplasia. Serological biomarkers may help identify individuals who should undergo endoscopy, although variation in assay thresholds and population characteristics limits their use for definitive risk staging. Artificial intelligence is also being explored to improve diagnostic consistency. In a multicentre pathology study, a deep-learning model achieved external-test AUCs of 0.884 for intestinal metaplasia and 0.877 for atrophy. Current evidence therefore favours combining these approaches according to their clinical roles rather than treating them as interchangeable tools: histology remains the basis of risk staging, endoscopy refines mucosal assessment and biopsy, biomarkers are most useful for triage, and artificial intelligence may support interpretation. Whether such integrated strategies improve surveillance efficiency or clinical outcomes still requires prospective, externally validated studies.

title: More Genes, Faster Inference: Efficient Large-Panel Spatial Transcriptomics Prediction from Histology
desc: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) prediction from histology aims to infer spatially resolved gene expression profiles directly from tissue images. This is a challenging problem that is currently often addressed with complicated model architectures, additional inputs, and complicated training procedures, while remaining limited to fixed, small gene panels. This raises a natural question: Is there an efficient method for large-panel ST prediction? Here, we present GeneFlow, a simpler yet effective framework for large-scale spatial gene expression prediction that unifies flow-matching generative modeling with structured multimodal fusion. Specifically, GeneFlow first encodes both histological morphology and cross-gene interactions in spatial spots through histology and gene tokenizers. The model directly predicts spatial gene expression, rather than an intermediate velocity field, while being trained with a velocity-based flow-matching objective. We show that, even without relying on heavy generative pipelines, GeneFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple ST benchmarks, with up to 56.8% gains in 1,000-gene prediction. Extensive experiments further show that GeneFlow produces biologically meaningful spot profiles while reducing computational cost by orders of magnitude, thereby improving efficiency and scalability, particularly in clinical settings. We believe GeneFlow provides an opportunity for leveraging widely available histology images for downstream biological discovery. Code is available at: https://github.com/ZZhangsm/GeneFlow

title: Performance of a Large Language Model for Predicting Clinical and Radiographic Outcomes in Knee Osteoarthritis: Single-Center Prospective Observational Study.
desc: [JMIR medical informatics] Large language models (LLMs) can extract information from unstructured clinical text, but it remains unclear whether their ability to assess current status translates into reliable predictions of longitudinal outcomes. This study aimed to evaluate DeepSeek's ability to assess baseline clinical and radiographic status in knee osteoarthritis (KOA), its performance in predicting 6-month outcomes, and its interrun reproducibility. This study used a single-center, prospective observational cohort design to conduct a blinded, retrospective evaluation of the LLM. A total of 128 patients with primary KOA were enrolled, of whom 111 (86.7%) completed the 6-month follow-up and were included in the primary analysis. DeepSeek-V4-Flash and a rheumatologist independently assessed KOA diagnoses, baseline Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) scores, and Kellgren-Lawrence (KL) grading based on the same standardized interview records and imaging reports and predicted 6-month outcomes. The LLM was run independently 3 times. The actual outcomes determined by another senior physician served as the reference, and the results were compared with the physician's predictions and the persistence model. The LLM showed high baseline diagnostic agreement with the physician (105/111, 94.6%) and good agreement on the WOMAC and KL, but 6-month predictions (WOMAC mean absolute error=5.92-6.58; KL exact agreement=74/111, 66.7%-76/111, 68.5%) were worse than those of the physician comparator (mean absolute error=3.86; 96/111, 86.5%) and not superior to those of the persistence model (mean absolute error=5.43). Despite high interrun intraclass correlation coefficients (0.982 and 0.965), exact agreement between runs was poor (35/111, 31.5% and 7/111, 6.3%). The evaluated DeepSeek configuration may support structured baseline KOA assessment. However, its 6-month predictive accuracy and patient-level stability remain limited. Prognostic applications require evidence of added value over a persistence model.

title: Electrocardiographic Imaging via Posterior Sampling under Operator Discrepancy
desc: Electrocardiographic imaging (ECGI) reconstructs heart-surface potentials from body-surface potentials, an ill-posed inverse problem. Diffusion posterior samplers combine a learned prior with an explicit forward operator that they assume to be accurate. In ECGI this operator is only an estimate, because the body changes with respiration and posture, and body composition such as subcutaneous fat is rarely known for an individual patient. The resulting operator discrepancy is structured and depends on the heart signal. We introduce OpDis-PS, a diffusion posterior sampler that models this discrepancy instead of treating it as signal-independent noise. OpDis-PS learns how the discrepancy depends on the signal, folds this into a corrected forward operator, and reconstructs with a fixed prior across all operator conditions. We study two realistic sources of discrepancy, changing lung conductivity and an added subcutaneous-fat layer. Across both, OpDis-PS reconstructs more accurately than classical regularization and learned predictors, with its largest gains on held-out cardiac pathologies.

title: Future directions of nanocatalysts in precision medicine: from catalytic therapy to intelligent nanozymes.
desc: [Discover nano] The scope of nanomedicine may be broadened by nanocatalysts, which can actively modulate biochemical reactions in vivo. Of these nanocatalysts, nanozymes (nanomaterials with intrinsic enzyme-like activity) probably have received the most attention. Their activity can catalyze a reaction similar to peroxidase, catalase, oxidase, superoxide dismutase, or glutathione peroxidase, depending on composition, thus generating or scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS) depending on the microenvironment. This review sketches the evolution of this field from first generation iron oxide nanozymes to more recent stimuli-responsive multi-enzyme nanostructures. Moreover, selected experimental studies are examined, starting from in vivo Fenton and Fenton-like chemodynamic therapy and cascade catalysis and oxygen-releasing nanozymes in cancer, to antioxidant, antimicrobial, and immunomodulatory nanozymes in regenerative medicine, neurological, cardiovascular, and infectious disease models, respectively. For every case, the specific nanozyme, the biological model, the proposed mechanism of action, and the primary results are outlined, while the amount of evidence supporting the work is rated. The challenges for translating these systems into the clinic are addressed, such as the selectivity of the catalytic process to the physiological H2O2 concentration, efficiency of biodistribution, availability of long-term safety studies, batch-to-batch consistency, and ambiguity on regulatory pathways. It is speculated which of these issues can be practically solved by machine learning and which are more resistant. Future strategies are envisioned in creating biohybrid, logic-gated nanozymes, omics-guided design, and in vitro autonomous discovery platforms. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: Not applicable. This study does not involve any clinical trial and does not require trial registration.

title: Where to Predict in Retinal OCT? Anatomy-Guided Target Selection for I-JEPA
desc: Self-supervised learning aims to learn meaningful representations from unlabeled data, potentially allowing models to capture subtle anatomical variations across patients and reduce the amount of labeled data needed. Image-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (I-JEPA) learns by predicting target-region representations from visible context rather than reconstructing pixels. However, its uniform target placement does not account for the anatomical structure of retinal OCT, where retinal tissue occupies only part of each B-scan. We investigate anatomy-guided target selection using image intensity and predicted retinal segmentation while retaining the I-JEPA architecture and latent prediction objective. We compare anatomy-guided rectangular targets, anatomy-shaped targets and coverage-constrained placement with uniform masking, and evaluate the learned representations using linear probing for glaucoma classification on FairVision. We found that rectangular targets guided by image intensity achieved the highest linear-probe AUC in our comparisons. We show that anatomically meaningful target selection is promising for retinal OCT representation learning, while greater anatomical specificity did not consistently improve performance.

title: AI Governance in Health Information Practice: A Practical Framework for HIPAA-Compliant AI Adoption.
source: PubMed · Advances in health information science and practice
desc: [Advances in health information science and practice] Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly being integrated into health information workflows, including clinical documentation, coding support, revenue cycle operations, and patient engagement systems. While these technologies offer efficiency and enhanced decision support, their use introduces new privacy, security, and compliance risks when protected health information is entered as input, processed by third-party systems, or incorporated into AI-generated outputs. Existing Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) compliance structures do not address the complexities of AI-enabled environments, creating governance gaps that expose health care organizations to regulatory and operational risk. This article presents a practical governance framework that integrates AI oversight into existing HIPAA compliance programs. Drawing on compliance literature, regulatory guidance, and emerging AI governance models, the framework adapts core elements of the Office of Inspector General compliance model to address AI-specific risks. We proposed AI-centered policies and procedures, governance leadership, workforce training, auditing and monitoring, and incident response planning. This article provides implementation guidance tailored to health information practice, including workflow-based examples and phased adoption strategies. By positioning AI governance as an extension of established information governance responsibilities, health information professionals can proactively safeguard patient privacy, strengthen regulatory compliance, and support responsible innovation in AI-enabled health care environments.

title: Continuous Cuffless Blood Pressure Estimation Using PPG From Methods to Clinical Translation
desc: Continuous blood pressure (BP) monitoring could improve hypertension management by capturing changes that intermittent cuff measurements miss. Photoplethysmography (PPG) is widely explored for cuffless BP estimation because optical sensors are inexpensive, wearable, and already present in many consumer and clinical devices. PPG, however, does not measure arterial pressure: BP is inferred from waveform characteristics or pulse timing, which also depend on vascular tone, arterial stiffness, sensor contact, motion, and individual physiology. This survey reviews PPG-based cuffless BP estimation along the full measurement chain, covering physiological mechanisms, waveform features, pulse arrival time (PAT), pulse transit time (PTT), machine-learning methods, datasets, calibration, validation, deployment, bias, and clinical translation. Studies are assessed by the strength of evidence they provide rather than by reported error alone, with particular attention to subject and temporal leakage, dataset imbalance, calibration dependence and drift, motion artifacts, and the gap between benchmark accuracy and reliable real-world measurement. The review finds that progress depends on more than better prediction algorithms. Future work should prioritize physiologically informed models, diverse longitudinal datasets, transparent reporting of calibration requirements and failure rates, stronger evaluation protocols, and studies that demonstrate practical value in clinical care.

title: Personas shift clinical action thresholds in large language models.
desc: [npj health systems] Clinical large language model (LLM) deployment is shifting from feasibility to liability, while current guidance largely treats model behavior as a control problem. We tested whether decision-style system prompts shift clinical action thresholds when clinical facts are held constant, and whether these shifts are consistent across settings and models. We defined nine physician personas by crossing three ethical orientations (duty-based, care-based, utilitarian) with three cognitive styles (intuitive, integrative, analytic). Twenty open-weight LLMs were evaluated on 2500 simulated emergency department vignettes and 2500 MIMIC-IV-Note discharge summaries. For each text, models answered five binary decision items (safety, autonomy, treatment, resource use, follow-up). Each condition was repeated ten times, yielding 5,000,000 total decisions. Under baseline prompting, models answered "Yes" to 42.8% of decisions. Persona prompts shifted affirmative rates from 36.9% to 46.4%, a 9.5 percentage-point swing under fixed clinical evidence. Effects were largest in autonomy and treatment and were consistent across corpora (85.7% directional agreement; r = 0.82 for effect sizes). Susceptibility varied by model (4.9-16.1 points), with no consistent protection from medical fine-tuning or model size. Decision-style system prompts reliably change clinical action thresholds in LLMs under fixed evidence. Prompting is a policy-setting layer, not just a communication layer, and should be treated as a first-class deployment configuration.

title: Alignment with Reflect-Reasoning: Learning How To Follow Principles
desc: The appropriate governing norms and principles for the alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) often depend on cultural context and deployment application. However, most alignment techniques focus on training models to conform to human preferences or constitutional principles specified at training time and subsequently fixed. In practice, many deployers rely on system prompting to implement contextual norms and guardrails at inference time. Prior work has shown that post-generation reflective reasoning with critique and revision can improve conformance compared to simple system prompting, but such methods are limited to the reasoning abilities inherent in the trained model. We introduce Reflect-Reasoning, a training method that teaches models how to reason about alignment to principles, rather than simply which principles to follow. Across five models, Reflect-Reasoning consistently outperforms both system prompting and explicit prompting strategies for in-context reflective reasoning. These improvements extend and generalize to entirely out-of-distribution domains of medical and financial principles. We additionally demonstrate that Reflect-Reasoning reduces the occurrence of rare but serious principle violations. Finally, we show that Reflect-Reasoning does not erode the safety engineering of a model and is robust against jailbreaking attempts using adversarial constitutions. Overall, our results demonstrate that Reflect-Reasoning is a scalable method for training constitutional alignment as a generalizable reasoning capability, enabling models to adapt to novel principles and produce transparent reasoning traces without additional fine-tuning.

title: Preoperative prediction of lymphovascular space invasion in early-stage cervical cancer using a deep learning-based 3D super-resolution MRI radiomics model.
desc: [BMC cancer] Lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI) is a critical prognostic factor guiding adjuvant therapy in early-stage cervical cancer, yet its preoperative assessment is often limited by the spatial resolution of standard MRI. This study aimed to investigate the value of a deep learning-based 3D super-resolution (SR) MRI radiomics model in predicting LVSI and to evaluate how SR reconstruction impacts image quality and radiomic feature robustness. This retrospective study included 117 patients with early-stage cervical cancer (training cohort: n = 81; validation cohort: n = 36). A 3D Super-Resolution Generative Adversarial Network (SRGAN) reconstructed T2-SPAIR and DWI sequences into super-resolution images (SRI) with a 4× upsampling factor. Radiomic features were extracted, and an SRI-based multimodal fusion model was developed and systematically compared with original image (OI)-based and clinical models using the Area Under the Curve (AUC) and Decision Curve Analysis (DCA). SR reconstruction significantly improved the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for both DWI (P = 0.012) and T2-SPAIR (P = 0.030). For DWI, SRI preserved intratumoral texture heterogeneity, leading to improved diagnostic performance (Validation AUC: SRI-DWI 0.864 vs. OI-DWI 0.727, P = 0.041). The final SRI-Fusion model achieved the highest diagnostic accuracy (Validation AUC: 0.934), significantly outperforming the OI-Fusion model (AUC: 0.828, P = 0.044) and the clinical model (AUC: 0.626, P = 0.012). SRGAN-based reconstruction effectively improves MRI quality and feature robustness, particularly in DWI. The SRI-based multimodal radiomics model demonstrates superior predictive performance for LVSI in early-stage cervical cancer compared to conventional imaging and clinical models.

title: Neural Simulation-Based Inference for Computational Cognitive Models: A Tutorial
desc: Computational cognitive modeling is an increasingly essential methodology to elucidate the mechanisms underlying human and animal cognition. By fitting models to empirical data, researchers can perform parameter estimation, model comparison, and model-based neural analyses to assess competing theories, quantify individual differences, and investigate neural representations. Typically, fitting these models relies on likelihood-dependent methods (e.g., Maximum likelihood estimation or hierarchical Bayesian methods). However, for many reasonable cognitive models, computing the likelihood is computationally intractable, in which case these methods become inadequate. This substantially limits the range of theories that researchers can investigate. Simulation-based inference with neural networks (neural SBI) has emerged as a powerful toolkit to overcome this hurdle. By training deep neural networks on datasets generated through model simulations, neural SBI learns the relation between observable data and cognitive models. This approach enables all the applications of standard modeling while bypassing the likelihood computation, without constraints on empirical data size. Despite its successful adoption across diverse scientific fields, neural SBI remains underutilized in cognitive modeling, partly due to a lack of accessible, domain-tailored guidance. This tutorial addresses this gap by providing a clear workflow for applying neural SBI to cognitive models. We also provide practical use cases and recommendations for reducing the computational and simulation burden, facilitating efficient implementation in real-world research settings. By lowering the technical barriers to neural SBI, this tutorial aims to empower cognitive scientists to investigate richer theory spaces and ultimately propel scientific discovery.

title: In silico drug discovery framework leveraging biomedical foundation models and evaluating generative models-a use case on 3CLpro.
source: PubMed · Journal of computer-aided molecular design
desc: [Journal of computer-aided molecular design] AI models such as foundation models and generative models have shown promise for aiding drug discovery alongside traditional cheminformatics and bioinformatics tools and physics-based approaches. In this study, we design a workflow that integrates these AI methods to generate molecules alongside established informatic and predictive filtering approaches to streamline downselection of molecules from the massive and noisy result sets generated by AI. This workflow evaluates generative methods based on validity, reliability, diversity, similarity, hallucination and campaign needs. Analyses are made on the original proprietary dataset to determine molecular property thresholds for screening criteria. Overall, 249 molecules are selected from ~ 5 million generated molecules. 18 molecules are then validated with free energy perturbation simulations. 5 out of 5 retain on target inhibition, with IC50 values below 1 μM. 1 of the 5 experimentally validated molecules displayed greater inhibition than the corresponding lead molecule. Predictive foundation model MMELON yields Pearson correlation R = 0.72 in blind test, showing potential for future drug discovery campaigns.

title: Artificial intelligence and clinical reasoning - a qualitative study with general practice trainees in Germany.
desc: [BMC medical education] General practitioners face high complexity in clinical decision-making. Large language models (LLMs) may support clinical reasoning, but their impact on decision-making processes and postgraduate medical training remains unclear. This qualitative study aims to explore General Practice (GP) trainee's use of LLMs in clinical reasoning and their educational needs. GP trainees were recruited and interviewed with semi-structured interview-guide. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and analysed qualitatively. Seventeen GP trainees participated (mean interview duration: 38 min; range: 21-63 min). AI was perceived as a tool to augment and accelerate clinical decision-making, while potential risks of deskilling were identified. Participants reported a lack of structured AI education and expressed a need for its integration into postgraduate training. Participants perceived AI primarily as a supportive tool that can complement clinical reasoning and improve access to medical knowledge. At the same time, they identified potential risks, including overreliance on AI-generated information and possible effects on the development of clinical expertise. These findings suggest that postgraduate medical training should address AI-related competencies, including critical appraisal, ethical responsibility and appropriate integration of AI into clinical decision-making. AI is already part of clinical practice among GP trainees, offering opportunities to support learning and clinical reasoning while raising concerns about overreliance and critical appraisal. Postgraduate medical training in GP should therefore incorporate structured AI competencies to ensure responsible, reflective and patient-centered use of AI.

title: Artificial Intelligence Models to Predict Recurrence in Patients with Differentiated Thyroid Cancer: A PROBAST + AI Systematic Review of Clinical Applicability.
source: PubMed · Thyroid : official journal of the American Thyroid Association
desc: [Thyroid : official journal of the American Thyroid Association] Differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC) generally carries an excellent prognosis, yet recurrence occurs in up to 8-9% of patients. Artificial intelligence (AI) models are increasingly proposed to predict DTC recurrence; however, their methodological quality and clinical readiness are poorly defined. We conducted a systematic review to evaluate the methodological quality, risk of bias, and applicability of these models using the PROBAST + AI framework. We searched Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane databases, Scopus, and Web of Science from inception to July 13, 2026. Eligible studies included original research developing or validating AI models for recurrence in DTC. Model quality (for development), risk of bias (for evaluation), and applicability were assessed using the PROBAST + AI framework, with a focus on discrimination, calibration, and validation strategies (PROSPERO; registration number [CRD420251004644]). Of 673 records screened, 34 studies were included (21 unique datasets and 13 UCI-derived publications), encompassing 21,267 patients with a recurrence rate of 7.8%. Most were developed in Asian cohorts (17 of 21 datasets) and were structured clinical/tabular variables (82.4%), including demographic, clinical, laboratory, and pathological data, whereas the remaining models incorporated multimodal inputs such as imaging-derived or radiomic features. Notably, nearly one quarter of included studies (13 of 34, 38%) represented reanalysis of a single dataset. Discrimination was reported in 22 of 34 studies (64.7%) (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] 0.67-1.00), though only 10 studies assessed calibration, none with standardized metrics. The PROBAST + AI assessment revealed high overall quality concerns in 26 of 34 (76.5%) development studies due to reliance on single-center cohorts, inadequate handling of missing data, and absence of external validation. Only 6 of 34 included studies (17.6%) were judged to have low overall quality concern, whereas 17 of 34 (50.0%) were rated as having low applicability concern. AI models for predicting DTC recurrence show promising discriminatory performance but have substantial methodological shortcomings in development, and a lack of calibration and external validation necessary for clinical use. Given the guidelines' emphasis on risk-adapted de-escalation of therapy, the development of robust, validated, and clinically calibrated AI tools is a priority. title: End-to-end deep learning for identifying Alzheimer's disease signatures in spectral fluorescence imaging of normal-appearing brain regions in 5xFAD mice.
source: PubMed · Journal of medical imaging (Bellingham, Wash.)
desc: [Journal of medical imaging (Bellingham, Wash.)] Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the leading cause of dementia, characterized by the accumulation of amyloid- β and tau aggregates in the brain. Current diagnostic approaches primarily detect mature plaques, but growing evidence suggests that pre-fibrillar aggregates are present earlier in normal-appearing tissue and may provide a valuable window for intervention. We propose the first proof-of-concept end-to-end deep learning (DL) model to identify AD signatures directly from normal-appearing tissue (i.e., background parenchyma) of raw spectral fluorescence data. To develop and evaluate our DL model, we used one million signals extracted from spectral fluorescence images of brain cortex sections collected from wild-type and 5xFAD mice (a transgenic strain carrying five familial human AD mutations). Our results demonstrate that AD-related signatures can indeed be detected in normal-appearing brain cortex regions. Experiments revealed that model performance depends on input dimensions, training set size, and the preprocessing kernel size. The optimal configuration used 1000 × 32 input, 9000 training samples, and a 3 × 3 kernel, achieving ≥ 95 % accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F 1 -score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Importantly, no mice were misclassified, and saliency analysis indicated that a broad range of spectral fluorescence wavelengths contributed to the model's decisions. These findings highlight the potential of DL-based analysis of spectral fluorescence data to enable earlier detection of AD-related changes, supporting a shift toward a more proactive strategy for biomarker discovery.

title: AI-assisted literature mining of perovskite ink formulations using a hybrid regex-LLM extraction pipeline.
desc: [RSC advances] Reproducibility of perovskite solar cell and LED fabrication depends critically on ink formulation details that are typically buried in the Methods sections of scientific articles. Manual curation of such data is slow, inconsistent, and does not scale. Here we present an end-to-end automated AI-assisted pipeline that (i) queries the OpenAlex academic graph to identify open-access publications containing perovskite ink formulations, (ii) downloads and parses PDF full texts using rule-based regex extraction, (iii) applies a large language model (LLM, Claude Haiku 4.5) as a second extraction layer to recover structured perovskite formulas, cleaned molarity values, and novel additive chemistries missed by regex, (iv) assigns a multi-criteria confidence score to each extracted recipe, and (v) exports a structured, analysis-ready dataset in tidy format. Applied to a corpus of 1041 screened publications, the pipeline recovered 68 annotated ink formulations from 71 successfully retrieved PDFs. The LLM extraction layer identified 46 structured perovskite formulas (31 unique compositions, including mixed-cation and quasi-2D types), increased molarity coverage from 49% to 60%, and increased high-confidence extractions from 32 (regex, score ≥7) to 36 (LLM confidence = high). Twenty records are automatically promoted and manually validated as the GOLD standard. The published data encompass 44 publication venues, and research articles published between 2014 and 2025, which record solvent systems, precursor stoichiometry, molarity, and additive solvent chemistry of halide perovskite inks. All code and data are freely available to accelerate materials informatics in this field.

title: Phenylpropanoid Amides from Buteae monospermae Semen as Hepcidin-Modulating Candidates for Anemia of Inflammation: Network Pharmacology, Deep Learning Prediction, and In Vitro Validation.
desc: [Molecules (Basel, Switzerland)] Anemia of inflammation (AI) is largely driven by interleukin-6 (IL-6)-induced hepcidin overproduction, which disrupts systemic iron homeostasis. Buteae monospermae Semen (BMS), the seeds of Butea monosperma (Lam.) Kuntze and a traditional Tibetan medicine, has long been used for blood-related disorders, yet its active constituents against AI remain unclear. Here, an integrated strategy combining ADMET screening, network pharmacology, deep learning-based affinity prediction, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and in vitro validation was applied to 58 BMS-derived compounds. Forty-three candidates with acceptable ADMET profiles were retained, and their predicted targets were enriched in inflammation- and iron metabolism-related pathways, particularly IL-6/JAK2/STAT3 signaling. Two phenylpropanoid amides, compounds 16 and 21, were prioritized and shown to interact favorably with hepcidin-related regulatory targets. In IL-6-stimulated HepG2 cells, both compounds dose-dependently reduced hepcidin levels (EC50 = 2.486 and 14.49 μM), with therapeutic indices of 4.40 and 33.7, respectively. These findings identify BMS-derived phenylpropanoid amides as hepcidin-modulating candidates for AI and demonstrate an effective computational-experimental strategy for discovering bioactive compounds from traditional medicines.

title: Design and Simulation of an AI-Powered Artificial Pancreas System With Personalized Glucose Sensing and Insulin Delivery.
desc: [Artificial organs] Achieving tight glycemic control in Type 1 diabetes is challenged by non-linear metabolic dynamics and insulin-stacking risk. Artificial intelligence models offer improved personalization, but their opacity raises safety concerns, particularly for basal insulin dosing, which is often treated as static in existing decision-support systems. We propose a hybrid closed-loop system combining a data-driven LightGBM regressor for basal dose prediction, trained on the T1D-UOM dataset, with a physiologically grounded, rule-based safety layer at the edge. Basal insulin is predicted from cyclical time encoding and glucose rate-of-change; bolus dosing follows carbohydrate intake and correction requirements. A time-bounded insulin-on-board model, an uncertainty-adaptive post-bolus damping factor, and a predictive low-glucose-suspend rule reproducing the Tandem Basal-IQ protocol together suspend or reduce delivery when residual insulin is high or hypoglycemia is projected. The system was evaluated in silico over 60 continuous days under shadow-mode replay and closed-loop reduced-order simulation, including an ablation with bolus delivery suppressed. Under chronological, within-subject validation, the offline basal estimator achieved R 2 = 0.68 and MAE = 0.21 U; under strict leave-one-subject-out validation on the same real cohort, performance did not generalize to unseen subjects ( R 2 = - 0.49 , MAE = 0.49 U). The hybrid controller maintained Time-in-Range at 62.8% within the reduced-order closed-loop simulation, with no violations of the insulin-on-board suspension or damping rules; suppressing bolus delivery in an ablation within this simulation dropped Time-in-Range to 26.1%, indicating that, within the reduced-order model, bolus delivery is a determinant of simulated glycemic outcome. The proposed architecture demonstrates a safety-audited template for combining machine-learning basal prediction with clinically grounded dosing rules. Validation on real outcome data and physical hardware is identified as the next steps toward clinical translation.

title: The Potential of Large Language Models in Gynecologic Oncology Telephone Triage.
desc: [Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland)] Introduction: Nurse-led telephone triage, frequently guided by the United Kingdom Oncology Nursing Society (UKONS) tool, is a cornerstone of supportive oncology care, yet the appropriateness of triage decisions varies across settings. Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise in medical communication but remain unvalidated for autonomous clinical decision-making, particularly in gynecologic oncology, where remote and telephone-based care pose distinct challenges. Methods and Materials: Twenty fictitious case vignettes representing common treatment-related toxicities in gynecologic oncology were developed. Three board-certified gynecologic consultants independently assigned UKONS Red-Amber-Green (RAG) triage categories, reaching unanimous consensus that served as the reference standard. Vignettes were submitted verbatim, as single-turn queries with no follow-up prompting, to three publicly available LLMs (OpenEvidence, ChatGPT, Google Gemini). LLM responses were mapped to RAG categories and compared descriptively against the reference standard, stratified by treatment type and platform. Results: All three LLMs achieved 100% concordance with the reference standard for all Red cases across both treatment groups, with no high-acuity case downgraded to self-care. Discrepancies clustered at lower-acuity boundaries. In the chemotherapy-alone group, errors were limited to omission of an explicit 24-h follow-up window for 1 Amber-rated complaints. In the combined group, all LLMs over-triaged intermediate-risk complaints toward immediate or same-day evaluation; low-risk complaints showed more variable over-triage. Conclusions: LLMs identified unambiguous emergent gynecologic oncology symptoms, preserving the UKONS safety floor, but showed relatively reduced precision and a conservative over-triage bias at lower-acuity margins, especially in the combined-therapy collective. These findings support a supervised, adjunctive role for LLMs, rather than autonomous deployment, pending prospective validation.

title: All-optical sensing of dermal activity enables an AI-powered wearable ring for continuous stress monitoring.
desc: [Science advances] Electrodermal activity (EDA), a primary stress-sensing signal in today's wearables, requires skin-electrode contact that drifts and degrades over time, limiting long-term use. Here, we present an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered ring for all-optical sensing of dermal activity (ODA), using light rather than electrodes to track sweat gland activation, thereby enhancing durability and comfort. An optimized dual-wavelength design (960 and 1250 nanometers) captures perspiration dynamics while concurrently recording photoplethysmography. The ODA ring integrates temperature and motion sensors for multimodal monitoring with on-device inference. In correlation studies, ODA and EDA signals showed 86% agreement. In classification tasks, the ODA ring achieved 92.3% binary accuracy versus 77.95% for EDA. In multiclass tasks, ODA outperforms EDA by 100 to 74.58% (short term) and 89.72 to 43.20% (long term). On-device one-dimensional convolutional neural network inference enabled 87.53% autonomous accuracy. This electrode-free modality establishes a scalable, all-optical platform for rings, watches, and patches for accurate, robust, and long-term stress monitoring.

title: Decoding metabolic bottlenecks: Advanced technologies for key gene identification in microbial cell factories.
desc: [Biotechnology advances] Constructing efficient microbial cell factories is a crucial platform for the industrial production of high-value-added products, and precisely identifying the key genes that govern biosynthesis levels is a core step in overcoming productivity bottlenecks. However, due to the extensive and complex regulatory networks inherent in biological systems, accurately identifying these key genes has long posed substantial challenges. This review systematically summarizes two main technical routes currently used to identify key genes: prior-knowledge-guided prediction methods and phenotype-oriented screening approaches. On this basis, we compare the applicable scenarios and limitations of each technique. Subsequently, we highlight the enabling role of machine learning in key genes prediction, particularly its value in functional gene annotation and the construction of genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs). We also summarize the progress and potential improvements in multi-target iterative engineering tools. The integration and synergistic application of these technologies can effectively accelerate the iterative Design-Build-Test-Learn (DBTL) cycle, thereby providing a methodological foundation for the rational design and efficient engineering of next-generation microbial cell factories.
